title: "Forecasting, Budgeting, and What-If Analysis in Excel"

::: {.learning-objectives}
## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

1. Measure the relationship between two variables with correlation and regression in the Data Analysis ToolPak, and judge the result with R², p-values, and residuals.
2. Forecast with TREND and FORECAST.LINEAR, and evaluate a forecast by backtesting it against simple benchmark methods.
3. Compare actual results with a static and a flexible budget, and explain sales-volume and flexible-budget variances.
4. Build a contribution margin model with documented assumptions, and calculate break-even points.
5. Evaluate a decision with Scenario Manager, data tables, and Goal Seek, and describe how Solver finds the best plan under constraints.
:::


## Opening Scenario {.unnumbered}

The controller has read your analysis of the Furniture margin, and she is now preparing for the planning meeting for fiscal 2027. She has three requests. First, she needs a revenue forecast for the coming quarter that she can defend when the sales team pushes for a more optimistic number. Second, she wants to know how 2026 compared with the budget, because the budget will be the starting point for next year's plan and she suspects that some of its assumptions were wrong. Third, the sales team has proposed repeating the Furniture Seasonal Promotion, and she wants a recommendation based on what the promotion actually cost and what it would need to achieve to pay for itself. Each request asks what could happen rather than what did happen. This chapter teaches the Excel tools that answer such questions, and the discipline of testing a model before anyone relies on it.



## From Explaining to Predicting and Deciding

Chapter 1 introduced four types of analytics. The earlier chapters of Part II used the first two: descriptive analytics to summarize what happened, and diagnostic analytics to explain why the Furniture margin fell. This chapter turns to the other two. Predictive analytics estimates what is likely to happen, such as next quarter's revenue. Prescriptive analytics recommends what to do, such as whether to repeat a promotion or which products to make when capacity is short.

The move from description to prediction changes the nature of the work. A PivotTable of last quarter's revenue is a statement of fact that anyone can check against the records. A forecast of next quarter's revenue is an estimate that depends on assumptions about how the future will resemble the past, and a model of a promotion depends on assumptions about how customers will respond. Nobody can check a forecast against the records until the period is over. That is why this chapter pairs every modeling tool with a test: a residual plot that shows where a regression fails, a backtest that compares a forecast method with what actually happened, a flexible budget that separates a plan's volume assumption from its prices, and a documented list of the assumptions behind every model.


## Correlation and Regression

### Correlation

A correlation coefficient measures how closely two numeric variables move together along a straight line. It ranges from −1 to +1. A value near +1 means that the variables rise together, a value near −1 means that one falls as the other rises, and a value near 0 means that there is little linear relationship. In Excel, `=CORREL(array1, array2)` returns the coefficient for two columns of equal length. The Data Analysis ToolPak, an add-in that comes with Excel, calculates a correlation matrix for several variables at once: choose **Data > Data Analysis > Correlation**. To make the ToolPak available, choose **File > Options > Add-ins**, select **Excel Add-ins** in the **Manage** box, click **Go**, and check **Analysis ToolPak** (Microsoft, 2026d).

A correlation coefficient is easy to calculate and easy to misread. It measures only linear association, so two variables with a strong curved relationship can show a coefficient near zero. It says nothing about cause: two variables can move together because a third variable drives both. And it is sensitive to unusual observations. Charles River's monthly revenue illustrates the last point. The first month of the data, January 2024, is a start-up month in which the company issued about half as many invoices as in a normal month. With that month included, monthly revenue appears strongly correlated with the number of customers invoiced. Without it, the correlation is much weaker, and revenue correlates more strongly with the average size of an invoice line instead. One month out of thirty-six changes the conclusion, which is a reason to look at the data before reading any coefficient.

### Simple Linear Regression

Simple linear regression fits the straight line `y = a + bx` that minimizes the squared vertical distances between the data points and the line. The dependent variable, y, is the one you want to explain or predict, and the independent variable, x, is the one you use to explain it. The intercept, a, is the value of the line when x is zero, and the slope, b, is the change in y for each one-unit increase in x. In accounting, regression is used to separate the fixed and variable parts of a mixed cost, to model how an expense moves with activity, and to develop the expectations that auditors compare with recorded amounts. Datar and Rajan (2021) treat it as one of the quantitative methods for estimating how costs behave.

The ToolPak's Regression tool, under **Data > Data Analysis > Regression**, reports three groups of results, which @fig-07-02 shows for Charles River's monthly revenue. The regression statistics measure the fit. R Square is the share of the variation in y that the line explains, from 0 to 1, and the standard error measures the typical distance of a point from the line, in the units of y. The ANOVA table tests whether the line explains more than chance would. The coefficients table gives the intercept and slope, each with a standard error, a t statistic, a p-value, and a 95 percent confidence interval. The p-value is the probability of seeing a slope at least as far from zero as the estimate if the true slope were zero, and a value below 0.05 is the conventional threshold for calling a relationship statistically significant.

![Monthly Revenue with Two Fitted Trends.](/visuals/svg/fig-07-01-monthly-revenue-trend.svg){#fig-07-01 fig-alt="A line chart of Charles River's monthly invoiced revenue from January 2024 to December 2026, with two straight trend lines. Revenue moves up and down within a narrow band in almost every month, but the first month, January 2024, labeled as the start-up month, is far below the rest. A dashed trend line fitted to all thirty-six months slopes upward noticeably, while a solid trend line fitted without January 2024 is nearly flat. The legend gives the R Square of each line, both of them low."}

![Regression Output from the Data Analysis ToolPak.](/visuals/svg/fig-07-02-regression-output.svg){#fig-07-02 fig-alt="A mock of the ToolPak's summary output for a regression of monthly revenue on a month index. It shows the regression statistics, including a low R Square; the ANOVA table with its Significance F; and the coefficients table for the intercept and the month index, with standard errors, t statistics, p-values, and 95 percent confidence limits. Four numbered markers outline the R Square, the Significance F, the slope, and the slope's p-value, and a legend explains each."}

Two further checks belong with every regression. The first is the residuals, the differences between the actual values and the line. A residual plot, which the Regression tool draws when you check **Residual Plots**, should look like a patternless band around zero. A single point far from the rest, or a curve in the residuals, means that the line describes the data poorly. The second check is the influence of individual points. As @fig-07-01 shows, the line fitted to all thirty-six months of Charles River's revenue slopes upward, and its slope is statistically significant, but almost all of that slope comes from the start-up month. Fitted without January 2024, the line is nearly flat, and its slope is no longer significant.

::: {.callout-warning .watch-out icon=false}
## Watch out
A statistically significant slope is not proof of a trend. A single unusual observation at one end of the data can tilt a line enough to make its slope significant, and Anscombe (1973) showed that data sets with identical regression lines and fit statistics can look nothing alike when they are plotted. Plot the data and the residuals before you report a regression, investigate any point that stands apart, and report the result both with and without it when it cannot be explained away.
:::


## Forecasting and Backtesting

### Trend Functions

Excel has worksheet functions that apply a regression line without the ToolPak. `FORECAST.LINEAR(x, known_y's, known_x's)` returns the value of the least-squares line at a new x, such as the next month's index, and `TREND(known_y's, known_x's, new_x's)` returns the values for several new x's at once, spilling them into adjacent cells (Microsoft, 2026b). On a chart, **Add Trendline** draws the same line and can display its equation and R Square. These tools make a linear forecast quick to produce, which is exactly why it needs testing: extending a line into the future assumes that the pattern of the past continues, and that the pattern is a line.

### Benchmark Forecasts

A forecasting method is worth using only if it does better than the simplest alternatives. Hyndman and Athanasopoulos (2021) describe four such benchmarks and recommend comparing every new method with them, because a method that cannot beat them is not worth considering. @tbl-07-01 lists them with their Excel equivalents.

| Method | Forecast for every future period | Excel example | Works well when |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mean | The average of the historical values | `=AVERAGE(C3:C34)` | The series fluctuates around a stable level |
| Naive | The last observed value | `=C34` | The series wanders without a stable level |
| Seasonal naive | The value of the same season last year | `=C23` for the same month or quarter a year earlier | There is a strong seasonal pattern |
| Drift or trend | The last value or the fitted line, extended by the average change | `FORECAST.LINEAR` or `TREND`, as in Tutorial 7.1 | The series grows or shrinks steadily |

: Benchmark forecasting methods {#tbl-07-01}

### Backtesting

A backtest evaluates a forecasting method on data that already has an answer. You fit the method to an earlier part of the history, forecast a later part that you held back, and compare the forecasts with what actually happened. The forecast error is the difference between the forecast and the actual value, and it is often expressed as a percentage of the actual, so that errors for periods or product lines of different size can be compared. The mean absolute percentage error averages those percentages, ignoring their sign, over the periods forecast. Charles River's data ends at December 2026, so the most recent quarter with actual results, the fourth quarter of 2026, is the natural holdout. A backtest cannot guarantee that a method will work in the future, but a method that fails on the recent past should not be trusted with the next quarter.

::: {.callout-tip .in-practice icon=false}
## In Practice
Budgets are negotiated as well as calculated. Managers who are evaluated against a budget have a reason to build slack into it, by underestimating revenue or overestimating costs so that the target is easier to meet (Datar & Rajan, 2021), while others push for optimistic plans that justify more resources. A statistical benchmark and a record of past forecast errors give the finance team an objective reference point for that discussion. The question to ask of any forecast is how it would have performed if it had been used in the past.
:::

## Budgets, Flexible Budgets, and Variances

### The Master Budget and Its Drivers

A budget is a plan expressed in money. A master budget combines the operating budgets, for sales, production, purchasing, and expenses, with the financial budgets for cash and the balance sheet. Charles River's budget is recorded in two Tables. BudgetLine holds the detail, one row for each account, month, and where applicable item and cost center, and its DriverType column records how each amount was calculated. Revenue is forecast units multiplied by a planned net price, cost of goods sold is the same units at standard cost, sales commissions are forecast revenue multiplied by a commission rate, payroll taxes and benefits are salaries multiplied by a burden rate, and recurring expenses such as rent follow their own drivers. The Budget Table summarizes the lines by cost center and account.

Knowing the drivers tells you which parts of a budget can be tested separately. Charles River's operating-expense budget, for salaries, rent, depreciation, and the other recurring accounts, turns out to be close to what the company spent. The sales budget is built from two assumptions that can be checked one at a time: how many units would be sold, and at what price. For Charles River, the second assumption is close to reality and the first is not.

::: {.callout-warning .watch-out icon=false}
## Watch out
A summary does not always contain all of its detail. Charles River's Budget Table summarizes the budget by cost center, and the operating-expense lines that have no cost center, such as rent, utilities, and insurance, do not appear in it. A total taken from the summary is therefore smaller than the budget's true total. Before you rely on a summary table, reconcile it to its detail, as you did with invoice totals in Chapter 4. Exercise 7.2 asks you to do so.
:::

### Static and Flexible Budgets

A static budget is the budget prepared for a single, planned level of activity. Comparing actual results with it mixes two different questions: whether the company sold the volume it planned, and whether it earned the planned prices and incurred the planned costs on the volume it did sell. A flexible budget separates the two. It keeps the budget's prices and costs per unit but recalculates the budget at the actual volume, so that it shows what the results would have been if everything except volume had gone according to plan (Datar & Rajan, 2021). Variable costs change with volume in a flexible budget, while fixed costs stay at their budgeted amounts. @fig-07-04 shows the three levels of comparison, and @tbl-07-02 defines the two variances that connect them.

![Static Budget, Flexible Budget, and Actual Results.](/visuals/svg/fig-07-04-flexible-budget-levels.svg){#fig-07-04 fig-alt="A diagram of three boxes from left to right: the static budget, planned volume at planned prices and standard costs; the flexible budget, actual volume at planned prices and standard costs; and the actual results, actual volume at actual prices, costed at standard. Each box gives the Furniture margin for fiscal 2026, which is far lower in the flexible budget than in the static budget, and a little lower again in the actual results. Brackets between the boxes label the sales-volume variance, a very large unfavorable amount, and the flexible-budget variance, a much smaller unfavorable amount, with a note on what each measures."}

| Variance | Calculation | What it measures | Who usually answers for it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sales-volume variance | Flexible-budget margin minus static-budget margin | The effect of selling more or fewer units than planned, at planned margins | Sales and marketing, and whoever prepared the volume forecast |
| Flexible-budget variance | Actual margin minus flexible-budget margin | The effect of actual prices and costs differing from plan on the units actually sold | Pricing, purchasing, and production |

: The two variances between the budget levels {#tbl-07-02}

A static budget whose volume assumption is far from what happened says more about the forecast than about performance. Charles River's sales budget planned for several times the units the company sold. Its quantities come from a sales forecast, as its DriverType records, and the company's demand-planning forecast has also run well above actual orders in every year of the data, as Exercise 7.6 shows. Compared with that budget, every product line shows an enormous unfavorable variance that no pricing or cost decision could explain. Flexing the budget to the actual quantities removes the volume assumption and leaves the questions that managers can act on.

### Variable and Fixed Costs in the Budget

Flexing also applies to expenses. A sales commission that is a percentage of revenue is a variable cost, so its flexible budget is the budgeted rate multiplied by actual revenue, not the static budget amount. A cost driven by headcount or by contract, such as salaries or rent, is fixed over the range of activity in question and stays at its budgeted amount. Comparing each expense with the right benchmark matters: a commission expense well below the static budget looks like savings, but most of the difference only reflects the smaller volume of sales. The driver behind a budgeted amount can also be tested directly. Charles River budgeted payroll taxes and benefits at a fixed percentage of salaries, and dividing the actual expense by actual salaries shows whether that rate held.

## Cost-Volume-Profit Analysis and What-If Tools

### Contribution Margin and Break-Even

Cost-volume-profit analysis models how profit responds to volume when costs are divided into variable and fixed parts. The contribution margin is revenue minus variable costs, the amount left over to cover fixed costs and earn a profit, and the contribution margin ratio is the contribution margin divided by revenue. Profit is the contribution margin minus fixed costs. The break-even point is the volume or revenue at which profit is zero, so break-even revenue equals fixed costs divided by the contribution margin ratio, and the margin of safety is the amount by which actual or planned revenue exceeds break-even (Datar & Rajan, 2021).

Consider a generic example. A business with fixed costs of $600,000 a year and a contribution margin ratio of 40 percent breaks even at revenue of $1,500,000. If it expects revenue of $2,000,000, its margin of safety is $500,000, or a quarter of expected revenue, and it earns a profit of $200,000. A target profit works the same way: to earn $300,000, revenue must cover the fixed costs and the target, so it must reach ($600,000 + $300,000) / 0.40, or $2,250,000. Exercise 7.3 applies these relationships to Charles River, using the operating-expense budget as the fixed costs.

The same logic answers questions about a single decision. A price reduction lowers the contribution margin of every unit that receives it, so the volume must rise enough to replace the lost margin. The required increase depends only on the contribution margin before and after the change, not on fixed costs, which the decision does not affect. Tutorial 7.3 uses this to evaluate the Furniture Seasonal Promotion.

### What-If Tools

A model that separates its inputs from its calculations can answer what-if questions, and Excel provides tools for asking them systematically (Microsoft, 2026c). @tbl-07-04 summarizes them.

| Tool | Where to find it | Question it answers |
|---|---|---|
| Scenario Manager | **Data > What-If Analysis > Scenario Manager** | What are the results under each of several named sets of inputs? |
| Data table | **Data > What-If Analysis > Data Table** | How does a result change across a range of values of one or two inputs? |
| Goal Seek | **Data > What-If Analysis > Goal Seek** | What value of one input produces a target result? |
| Solver | **Data > Solver**, after loading the Solver add-in | What values of several inputs give the best result within a set of constraints? |

: Excel's what-if tools {#tbl-07-04}

Scenario Manager stores named scenarios, each a set of values for the changing cells, and its **Summary** button builds a report that compares the result cells across all of them. A data table recalculates a formula for every value in a row or column of inputs, or for every combination of two inputs, and fills in the results. Goal Seek works backward from a target: it changes one input cell until a formula cell reaches the value you specify, which makes it the quickest way to find a break-even point.

Solver extends Goal Seek to many inputs and to constraints. You specify an objective cell to maximize or minimize, the variable cells Solver may change, and the constraints the solution must satisfy, such as the hours available in each work center. For a linear model, the Simplex LP method finds the optimum (Microsoft, 2026a), and Solver can then produce a Sensitivity report that shows, among other things, how much the objective would improve with one more unit of each constrained resource, its shadow price. That report is available only when the model has no integer constraints (Frontline Systems, n.d.), so a production plan is usually solved first without requiring whole units. Exercise 7.4 builds such a model from Charles River's routings.

### Documenting Assumptions

A model is only as good as its assumptions, and an assumption that is not written down cannot be reviewed. Every model should state each key assumption, the value used, its source, and how sensitive the conclusion is to it. The sensitivity is what makes the documentation useful: an assumption that can move far without changing the recommendation needs little further evidence, while one that reverses the recommendation with a small change deserves the most scrutiny. Data tables and Goal Seek provide the evidence for that column, as Tutorial 7.3 shows.


{{< include _tutorial-03.qmd >}}


## Communicating Forecasts and Models

A forecast presented as a single number invites more confidence than it deserves. Report a range alongside the point estimate, such as the range of recent quarterly values or the forecast plus or minus its backtest error, and state the method and the period it was fitted to. A budget variance report should say which variances are meaningful and why: for Charles River, the sales-volume variance measures the forecast rather than the business, and the report is clearer if it says so in a sentence than if it leaves a reader to discover it. A recommendation from a model should state the assumption that matters most and how far it would have to move to change the answer.

Models also need maintenance. The inputs of the promotion model come from 2026 data, and a refresh of the workbook updates them, but the assumptions about customer behavior do not update themselves. Record in the workbook's documentation when each assumption was last reviewed, and revisit the assumptions whenever the results they produce stop matching what happens.

::: {.callout-note .connecting-dots icon=false}
## Connecting the Dots
The models in this chapter rest on the prepared, reconciled data of the earlier chapters: the invoice lines with their periods and product types, and the ledger totals you tested in Part I. The same questions recur in the later Parts of the book. A SQL query can produce the monthly series a forecast needs directly from the database, and an interactive report can present a variance analysis so that a manager can drill from a product line to its months. In every tool, a model deserves trust only after it has been tested against what actually happened.
:::


## Looking Ahead

This chapter has moved from explaining the past to estimating the future and evaluating decisions. You measured relationships with correlation and regression and learned to read the ToolPak's output, and you saw how a single unusual month can manufacture a trend. You forecast with trend functions and learned to judge a forecast by backtesting it against simple benchmarks. You compared 2026 with the budget, flexed the budget to the actual volume, and separated a volume assumption that failed from a price assumption that was only slightly optimistic. Finally, you built a contribution margin model, asked what-if questions of it with Scenario Manager, data tables, and Goal Seek, and documented the assumptions behind its recommendation.

The controller now has a forecast she can defend, an explanation of the budget variances, and a recommendation on the promotion. Along the way, you have also seen several conditions in the data that an auditor would want to examine more closely, from invoices whose dates and numbers disagree to a planning forecast that has run well above actual demand. The next chapter looks at the Charles River data through the auditor's eyes.
